Border Dispute with Brazil Roils Uruguay’s Economy as Tensions Mount

MONTEVIDEO – Economic activity across Uruguay has been disrupted by an escalating border dispute with Brazil, now entering its second week. The crisis began after Brazilian authorities established new customs checkpoints and restricted the transit of goods through the border towns of Rivera and Chuí, following a disagreement over water rights along the Yaguarón River.

Uruguayan exporters report delays of up to five days, with perishable goods like dairy and citrus especially affected. “We’re seeing trucks lined up for kilometers at the border,” said Martín Sosa, spokesperson for the Uruguayan Road Transport Association. “Many shipments are at risk of spoilage, and our drivers face uncertainty.”

The government estimates cross-border trade has dropped by more than 40% since the restrictions began, impacting thousands of jobs linked to logistics, warehousing, and export processing. “The situation is extremely serious,” said Minister of Economy Ana Bazán in a televised address. “Our government is in continuous talks with Brazilian counterparts, pressing for the immediate restoration of normal commerce.”

Supermarkets in northern departments such as Artigas and Cerro Largo report shortages of Brazilian-produced staples, with local shoppers expressing frustration. “We rely on both sides of the border to fill our shelves,” said Federico Méndez, manager of the El Ceibo supermarket chain. “Now we’re rationing products and prices are rising.”

The Uruguayan Chamber of Commerce has called for government intervention, warning that extended disruptions could ripple through the wider economy. Economic analyst Laura Bentancur noted, “Brazil is Uruguay’s largest trading partner. Any prolonged blockages will hit small businesses and consumers hard.”

No timeline has been given for a resolution. President Rodrigo Ferreyra has urged calm, assuring citizens that “all diplomatic channels remain open.” Meanwhile, demonstrations have broken out in Rivera and other affected towns, with local unions demanding swift action to restore cross-border trade.
